title: Migration by Numbers
sub: Grades 5–8 · Mathematics · The Great Migration in data
objective: Students will use real Great Migration population data to practice percentage change, data interpretation, ratio and proportion, and graphical representation. They will understand that mathematics can reveal the scale of historical events — and that the numbers behind the Harlem Renaissance represent millions of individual human decisions.
materials: Calculators (optional — Green level may benefit; Red level should work without)
Graph paper or handout graph grids (included on handouts)
Optional: project the Great Migration Map to give geographic context before the data work
connection: **Option 1 — Visit the exhibition:** bring your class to experience the phonograph, the Great Migration Map, the Jazz Lab, and more. Ask your librarian to arrange a visit.
**Option 2 — Virtual visit:** online at the address below.

steps.title: How big is a million?
script: *“Six million people moved north during the Great Migration. That’s a number that’s hard to visualize. Let’s try: imagine a school of about 650 students. How many schools that size would you need to fill to get 6 million students? Take 30 seconds and work it out.”*

screen.question: How many schools that size would you need to fill to get 6 million students?

steps.purpose: Make a number too big to picture into one you can.
students: Imagine a school of about 650 students.
Take 30 seconds and work it out.

steps.title: The answer
script: Answer: **~9,230 schools.** Then: *“Each one of those 6 million people made a decision — pack up, leave everything, travel north. Today we’re going to look at what those decisions look like in numbers.”*

examples.title: Six million students
steps: Imagine a school of about 650 students.
How many schools that size would you need to fill to get 6 million students?

steps.purpose: Turn the scale back into people: every one made a decision.
students: Each one of those 6 million people made a decision — pack up, leave everything, travel north.

steps.title: Reading the data
script: Walk through the core dataset on the board — Chicago’s Black population: 1910 (44,103), 1920 (109,458), 1930 (233,903), 1940 (277,731), 1950 (492,265), 1960 (812,637). Ask: before we calculate anything, what does this data tell us just by looking at it? What years show the fastest growth?
steps.purpose: Read the data before calculating anything.
students: Before we calculate anything, what does this data tell us just by looking at it?
What years show the fastest growth?

steps.title: Percentage change
script: *“Percentage change is the mathematician’s way of making fair comparisons. A city growing by 10,000 people means something very different if it started with 50,000 versus 5 million. We calculate: (new − old) ÷ old × 100.”*
steps.purpose: Learn the fair way to compare growth.
students: Which decade grew faster proportionally? Which added more people?

steps.title: Choose a handout

levels.name: Green Level
levels.summary: Read a pre-drawn bar chart of Chicago’s Black population growth. Identify the decade of fastest growth, calculate one percentage change with scaffolding, and answer interpretation questions in complete sentences.

levels.name: Yellow Level
levels.summary: Calculate percentage change for all six decades. Create a line graph from the data table. Identify and explain the pattern. Compare Chicago to one other Northern city using a ratio.

levels.name: Red Level
levels.summary: Full percentage change table for three cities (Chicago, New York, Detroit). Calculate rates of change. Analyze: which city’s Black population grew fastest proportionally vs absolutely? Write a statistical summary paragraph and evaluate what the data does not show.

steps.purpose: Work with the census data at the right level of challenge.
students: Choose Green, Yellow or Red. You can switch at any time.

steps.title: Closing
script: *“These numbers represent human beings. Every percentage point of growth is thousands of families who packed their belongings and moved north. Mathematics helps us understand the scale of history — but it can’t tell us what it felt like. That’s what the poets and painters were for.”*
steps.purpose: Return from the numbers to the people they count.
students: Numbers can tell us how many people moved. What can’t numbers tell us about the Great Migration?
